title: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
summary: Why analytic engines store columns and process vectors: Parquet row groups and stats, Arrow buffers, X100's vector-at-a-time model, selection vectors, SIMD and compiled-versus-vectorized tradeoffs.
outcomes: Compute how many bytes a scan reads in row versus column layouts and when the advantage disappears
Explain how a Parquet reader uses the footer, row groups and min/max statistics to skip data
Decode an Arrow validity bitmap and offsets buffer by hand
Explain why vector-at-a-time execution beats tuple-at-a-time and column-at-a-time, and how vector size is chosen
Choose between vectorized and compiled execution, and predict when SIMD selection pays off

lessons.title: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows

blocks.md:
A transactional workload (insert an order, read one customer) touches *all* columns of *few* rows. An analytic workload (total revenue per region last year) touches *few* columns of *many* rows. The physical layout that is best for one is poor for the other.

A **row store** keeps each row's fields next to each other on a page. The literature calls this the N-ary storage model (**NSM**). A **column store** keeps all values of one column next to each other, the decomposition storage model (**DSM**). The query is the same SQL either way; only the bytes the engine must touch differ.

blocks.title: SUM(price) over a 4-row table: row layout versus column layout

scenes.caption: The same 4-row table (id, name, price, qty) laid out two ways in memory. Assume, to keep it small, that one cache line or disk block holds 4 cells.
SUM(price) needs only pr0 to pr3. In the row layout they sit at positions 2, 6, 10 and 14, one per block, so the scan loads all 4 blocks to use 4 of 16 cells.
In the column layout the prices are contiguous at positions 8 to 11: one block, every byte useful. The other three blocks are never read.
The flip side: treat row 3 as a newly inserted row. In the row layout it is one contiguous record, but in the column layout its four values land in four separate column regions.

blocks.md: Scale this up with a simple model: a table of 6,000,000 rows (about the size of TPC-H `lineitem` at scale factor 1) with 16 columns of 8 bytes each, so 128 bytes per row. A row store must stream all 768 MB to scan it, no matter how many columns the query names. A column store reads 6,000,000 x 8 = 48 MB per column it needs.

blocks.title: Bytes scanned (MB) for 6M rows x 16 columns of 8 bytes

scenes.caption: Row store: every query streams the whole 768 MB, because the needed values are interleaved with the unneeded ones.
Column store: 48 MB per column touched. A 4-column query reads 192 MB, a 4x saving; the advantage vanishes only when the query needs every column.

blocks.prompt: In the row layout, scanning one 8-byte column of 128-byte rows from disk, what fraction of the bytes read is actually used?
blocks.reveal: 8 / 128 = **6.25%**. Disks and SSDs read whole pages (4 KB or more) that hold complete rows, so the other 93.75% is read and thrown away. In RAM the waste is similar: memory moves whole 64-byte cache lines (on typical x86 cores), so each 128-byte row costs at least one full line for its 8 useful bytes, at best 12.5% used. That waste costs bandwidth at every level: disk to RAM, RAM to cache, cache to registers.

blocks.md: Columns also **compress** better. All values in a column share one type and often a small set of values (a status flag, a country code, a date), so simple schemes like dictionary and run-length encoding work well. Abadi, Madden and Hachem measured that in the C-Store column store, compression can give order-of-magnitude gains when the data allows it, and that keeping data in columns late into the plan (*late materialization*) gave about a factor of 3 across their benchmark.

The costs are real too. MonetDB/X100's authors note that with vertical storage *a single row update or delete must perform one I/O for each column*. Their fix, used in some form by most analytic engines, is to treat the column fragments as immutable: deletes go into a deletion list, inserts go into small separate delta columns, and the system periodically reorganizes to fold the deltas back in. Reading a full row back also means fetching the value at the same position from every column, a step called **tuple reconstruction**.

Misconception: a column store is just a row store with one index per column. Abadi et al. tested exactly that (vertical partitioning and index-only plans in a commercial row store) and found it significantly slower, because the gains also come from the executor: compression-aware operators, late materialization and block-at-a-time processing.
Columns win when queries read few columns of many rows; rows win for point reads and frequent updates of whole records. The layout decides how many bytes a scan must move.

blocks.question: A dashboard query computes AVG(amount) and COUNT(*) grouped by region over 500 million rows of a 40-column table. What is the main reason a columnar layout helps?
options: It reads only the 2 needed columns instead of all 40, cutting bytes scanned roughly 20x
Column stores keep an index on every column, so the scan becomes index lookups
Each row is stored contiguously, so the CPU prefetcher works better
Columnar files are always smaller because they skip null values
blocks.explain: The query touches region and amount only. A column layout lets the scan skip the other 38 columns entirely, so it moves about 2/40 of the bytes (less after compression). No per-column index is needed; the win is the layout itself.

blocks.question: A service writes 50,000 single-row updates per second, each changing every field of a record. Which choice fits best?
options: A pure column store, because each column compresses better
A row store, or a column store that buffers writes in row-wise delta structures
A column store with a larger page size
Either; layout does not affect update cost
blocks.explain: Each update touches every column, so a pure column layout would write into one place per column. Row stores write one contiguous record. Column stores cope by sending writes to delta structures (as MonetDB/X100 does) and merging later.

lessons.title: Parquet on disk: row groups, column chunks, pages and a footer

blocks.md:
A pure column-per-file layout makes writing awkward: a writer would have to keep one open file per column. **Apache Parquet** uses a hybrid. It cuts the table horizontally into **row groups**; inside a row group, it stores one **column chunk** per column, contiguous in the file; each column chunk is split into **pages**, the unit of encoding and compression.

The Parquet docs give the units of parallelism directly: file or row group for splitting work across tasks, column chunk for I/O, page for encoding and compression.

blocks.title: Reading a Parquet file: footer first, then only the needed chunks

nodes.label:
File metadata
schema, chunk offsets, stats

scenes.caption: File layout per the spec: magic, then row groups (each holding one chunk per column), then the file metadata, its 4-byte little-endian length, and the magic again. Metadata comes last so a writer can produce the file in one pass.
A reader starts at the end: the last 8 bytes give the metadata length and the magic, so it knows exactly where the footer starts.
The footer lists every column chunk's byte offset and size, plus optional min and max statistics. The reader now plans its I/O without touching any data.
For SELECT SUM(price) WHERE shipdate >= X, it fetches only the shipdate and price chunks, and skips row group 1 entirely if its stats say no row can match.

blocks.md: The footer (Parquet calls it `FileMetaData`, defined in Thrift) holds, for each column chunk, a `ColumnMetaData` with the codec, the encodings used, `num_values`, compressed and uncompressed sizes, `data_page_offset`, and an optional `Statistics` struct with `min_value`, `max_value` and a null count. Those statistics let a reader prune whole row groups before reading them, often called *predicate pushdown* or *zone maps*.

blocks.title: Row-group pruning with min/max stats for WHERE shipdate >= 1997-06-01

scenes.caption: Four row groups of a file sorted by shipdate. Each has a min and max for the column in the footer (shown here as year-month).
A row group can contain a match only if its max is at least 1997-06-01. Groups 0 to 2 end before that date, so they are skipped without reading a byte of their data.
Same data written unsorted: every row group spans the full date range, so no min/max test can exclude any group and all four must be read. Pruning depends on how the data was clustered.

blocks.md:
Parquet also has an optional **page index** (`ColumnIndex` and `OffsetIndex`) stored near the footer. It keeps min and max per *page*, so a selective scan can skip individual pages, and offsets let the reader skip the matching rows in the other columns.

Inside pages, values are **encoded**. `PLAIN` writes values back to back. **Dictionary encoding** (`RLE_DICTIONARY`) writes each distinct value once in a dictionary page and stores the data as small integer ids using the **RLE/bit-packing hybrid**: runs of a repeated id are stored once with a count, other ids are packed with just enough bits each.

blocks.title: Bit-packing ids 0 to 7 at bit width 3 (Parquet spec example)

scenes.caption: Eight ids that each fit in 3 bits. Plain 32-bit storage would take 32 bytes.
Bit-packing fills each byte from its least significant bit up: values 0, 1 and the low 2 bits of value 2 form byte 0, binary 10001000 (0x88).
All 8 values occupy 24 bits, exactly 3 bytes: 10001000 11000110 11111010 (0x88 0xC6 0xFA). That is the spec's own worked example, reproduced by a script.

blocks.md: Work one column through. Take 1,000,000 values of a flag column with three distinct one-letter values. `PLAIN` byte arrays store a 4-byte length plus the byte: 5,000,000 bytes. With a dictionary, the 3 entries cost 15 bytes and each id needs $\lceil \log_2 3 \rceil = 2$ bits, so bit-packing alone gives about 250,000 bytes (ignoring run headers), roughly 20x smaller. If the data is sorted into 3 runs, RLE stores each run as a variable-length integer header (ULEB128, 3 bytes here) plus one value byte: 12 bytes of runs, plus the 1-byte bit width that starts a dictionary data page.

The spec recommends large row groups (512 MB to 1 GB) for long sequential reads, and about 8 KB data pages for finer-grained access. Real writers expose these as tuning knobs; smaller row groups make min/max pruning finer at the cost of more metadata.

blocks.question: A query filters on user_id = 42 over a 200 GB Parquet dataset written in arrival order (user_id random). Row-group stats show every group's min near 0 and max near the largest id. What will pruning achieve, and what fixes it?
options: Full pruning; min/max stats always locate a single value
Little pruning; sorting or clustering the data by user_id before writing makes min/max ranges narrow
Little pruning; switching from Snappy to Zstd compression fixes it
Full pruning, because dictionary encoding is applied to user_id
blocks.explain: Min/max stats can only exclude a group whose range misses the value. With random ids every range covers 42. Clustering by user_id narrows each range so most groups are skipped. The codec does not change the stats.

blocks.question: Why does Parquet put the file metadata at the end of the file instead of the start?
options: Readers must scan the data before they can parse the schema
So the writer can stream row groups out in a single pass and record their offsets and stats afterwards
Because Thrift requires trailing headers
To make appends to an existing file cheap
blocks.explain: The spec says metadata is written after the data to allow single-pass writing: chunk offsets and statistics are only known once the chunks are written. Readers simply read the last 8 bytes first.

lessons.title: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets

blocks.md:
Parquet is optimized for storage: encoded, compressed, read sequentially. To compute on data you decode it into an in-memory columnar form. **Apache Arrow** standardizes that form so different libraries and processes can share it without converting. The spec lists its goals: data adjacency for scans, O(1) random access, SIMD and vectorization friendliness, and relocatable buffers that allow zero-copy sharing, in exchange for more expensive mutation.

An Arrow **array** is a length, a null count, and a few flat **buffers**. A **record batch** is a set of equal-length arrays, one per column, with a schema.

scenes.caption: Values live in one contiguous buffer of 4-byte slots, so element j is at byte 4j: O(1) access. Null slots still occupy space; their contents are unspecified.
A separate validity bitmap holds one bit per slot: 1 means valid, 0 means null. Here the null count is 2.
Bits are numbered least-significant first, so slot 0 is the lowest bit. Reading byte 0 from bit 7 down gives 00110101, which is 0x35. Padding bits are 0.

blocks.caption: The validity test from the Arrow spec: byte j/8, bit j mod 8, least-significant bit first.

blocks.title: Summing an Arrow array while skipping nulls

scenes.caption: Setup: the bitmap byte 0x35 and the values buffer. Slots 1 and 3 hold garbage because they are null.
j = 0: bit 0 of 0x35 is 1, so slot 0 is valid and 7 is added.
j = 1: bit 1 is 0, so the garbage in slot 1 is ignored.
j = 2 and j = 3: 3 is added, slot 3 is null and skipped.
j = 4 and j = 5: 5 and 9 are added. Result 24 over 4 valid values. Real kernels test 64 bits at a time and skip the bit check when the null count is 0.

blocks.md: Variable-length values such as strings use two buffers. An **offsets** buffer holds length + 1 integers; value j occupies bytes `offsets[j]` to `offsets[j+1]` of a **data** buffer. For `['scan', null, 'vec', 'simd']` the offsets are `0, 4, 4, 7, 11` and the data buffer is the 11 bytes `scanvecsimd`. The null in slot 1 has length 4 minus 4 = 0, and the validity bitmap is 00001101.

blocks.prompt: Why store strings as one big data buffer plus offsets, instead of an array of pointers to separately allocated strings?
blocks.reveal: Pointers are only meaningful inside one process's address space, so an array of pointers cannot be written to a file, mapped by another process, or sent over the network without rewriting every pointer (*pointer swizzling*). Offsets are relative, so the same bytes are valid anywhere. That is what lets Arrow buffers be shared zero-copy, and it also keeps the string bytes contiguous for scans.

blocks.md: Arrow recommends allocating buffers on 64-byte boundaries and padding them to a multiple of 64 bytes. The spec says this matches the 512-bit width of AVX-512 registers, so a loop can process whole SIMD registers without a scalar tail check. Our 6-value Int32 array uses 24 bytes of values but sits in a 64-byte padded buffer.

Arrow is not a file format for long-term storage like Parquet. Arrow data is laid out for fast random access and computation and is normally uncompressed in memory (the IPC format allows only optional LZ4 or ZSTD buffer compression); Parquet is encoded and compressed for small size on disk. A typical pipeline reads Parquet and decodes it into Arrow-style (or engine-specific) column vectors.
A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

blocks.question: An Arrow Int8 array has validity bitmap byte 0 equal to 0b01000011 and length 7. Which slots are null?
options: Slots 0, 1 and 6
Slots 2, 3, 4 and 5
Slots 1, 6 and 7
Slots 0 and 1 only
blocks.explain: Least-significant bit first: bits 0 and 1 are set, bits 2 to 5 are clear, bit 6 is set. Set means valid, so slots 2, 3, 4 and 5 are null. Bit 7 is padding beyond the length.

blocks.question: A string array has offsets [0, 3, 3, 8, 10]. How long is the value in slot 2, and what can you conclude about slot 1?
options: Slot 2 has length 8; slot 1 is null
Slot 2 has length 3; slot 1 is invalid because offsets repeat
Slot 2 has length 5; slot 1 has length 0, so it is either null or the empty string (check the bitmap)
Slot 2 has length 2; slot 1 has length 3
blocks.explain: Length of slot j is offsets[j+1] minus offsets[j]: 8 minus 3 = 5 for slot 2, and 3 minus 3 = 0 for slot 1. Zero length alone does not tell null from empty string; only the validity bitmap does.

blocks.md: Storage is only half the story. Most engines run queries as a tree of operators using the **Volcano** iterator model: each operator has a `next()` method that returns one tuple, pulling from its children. It is simple and composable, but every tuple pays for virtual calls, and every expression is evaluated by an *interpreter* that walks an expression tree, because the operator only learns the column types and expressions at query time.

Boncz, Zukowski and Nes measured what that costs (CIDR 2005). In a profile of MySQL 4.1 running TPC-H Query 1, the five functions doing the real arithmetic and aggregation took under 10% of the time; 28% went to the aggregation hash table and most of the rest to record navigation and copying. A single addition (`Item_func_plus::val`) executed 38 instructions at an IPC (instructions per cycle) of about 0.8, which the paper estimates at about 49 cycles, versus a few cycles for a tight loop. Because each call does one addition, the compiler cannot overlap work across tuples (*loop pipelining*), and the call overhead is amortized over a single value.

MonetDB took the opposite extreme: **column-at-a-time**. Its MIL operators each process an entire column and write a fully materialized result column. Interpretation overhead disappears, but on Query 1 the authors found nearly every MIL operator was *memory-bound*: stuck at about 500 MB/s of RAM bandwidth on their machine, and almost twice as fast when the data was shrunk to fit in cache.

blocks.title: Order of work for select, compute, compute, aggregate

scenes.caption: Column-at-a-time (MonetDB/MIL): each operator runs over all 6M rows and writes a full intermediate column to RAM before the next starts. Simplified: shows ordering only, not measured time.
Tuple-at-a-time (Volcano): one row flows up the whole tree per round of next() calls. Nothing is materialized, but every row pays call and interpretation overhead at every operator.
Vector-at-a-time (X100): next() returns a vector of about 1000 values per column. Each operator runs a tight loop over the vector, and the intermediate stays in CPU cache for the next operator.

blocks.md: **MonetDB/X100** (the research system VectorWise, now Actian Vector, grew out of) strikes the balance: keep Volcano's pipelined `next()` interface, but pass small, cache-resident vertical chunks of each column called **vectors**. The per-call overhead is now paid once per vector, and the actual work happens in **primitives**: tiny type-specialized functions that loop over arrays, which compilers turn into pipelined (and often SIMD) machine code. In X100's Query 1 trace, a multiplication primitive ran at about 2.2 cycles per tuple, against roughly 49 for MySQL's per-tuple addition.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: w = work per tuple, c = per-vector call overhead, n = vector size, B = bytes of all live vectors per tuple, K = cache size, m = extra cycles when vectors spill to RAM.

blocks.title: Vector size sweet spot (simplified cost model)

scenes.caption: n = 1 is tuple-at-a-time: the overhead c dominates (103 cycles per tuple in this model). Growing n amortizes it quickly: about 3.8 cycles at n = 128 and 3.1 at n = 1024.

With K = 320 KB (the AthlonMP's combined L1 and L2 in the X100 paper) and about 40 bytes of vectors per tuple, the vectors fill the cache at n = 8192. Beyond that, intermediates spill to RAM and cost rises again.
At n = 4M the engine is effectively column-at-a-time and memory-bound again, about 23 cycles per tuple here. A 3 MB cache moves the knee out to about 78,600 tuples.

blocks.md: The real measurements match this shape. X100 used a default vector size of 1024; on Query 1 the best was around 1000, and anything from 128 to 8K worked well. At a vector size of 1 it suffered the same interpretation overhead as MySQL, and at very large sizes it behaved like MonetDB/MIL. Kersten et al. (VLDB 2018) found the same in their vectorized engine: vectors smaller than 64 or larger than 64K hurt significantly, and about 1,000 was a good setting for all queries except Q3, which ran 15% faster with 64K. DuckDB's default `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE` is 2048.

Vectorization keeps the iterator model but changes its unit from one tuple to a cache-sized vector. That amortizes interpretation overhead (small n is bad) without materializing whole columns in RAM (huge n is bad).

blocks.question: An engine uses vector size 1,000,000 and its query plan keeps about 60 bytes of live vectors per tuple. Its CPU has 2 MB of L2 per core. What do you predict?
options: It runs fastest, because overhead is amortized over a million values
It behaves like tuple-at-a-time, with high interpretation overhead
Vector size does not matter once primitives use SIMD
It behaves much like column-at-a-time: 60 MB of intermediates spill out of cache and execution becomes memory-bound
blocks.explain: 1,000,000 x 60 bytes is 60 MB, far beyond a 2 MB cache, so every intermediate is written to and re-read from RAM, like MonetDB/MIL. Overhead is already negligible by about 1,000 values; going bigger only adds cache misses.

blocks.question: In the MySQL profile from the X100 paper, why did one addition cost tens of cycles instead of about 3?
options: The MIPS CPU had no floating-point unit
Each call computed a single addition, so the dependent load-add-store chain could not overlap with other tuples and the call overhead was paid per value
Addition required a hash-table lookup
The data was compressed and needed decoding first
blocks.explain: The paper explains that with one addition per call the compiler cannot pipeline the loop, so four dependent instructions wait on each other (about 20 cycles), and the routine call adds a similar amount again.

lessons.title: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors

blocks.md:
Now follow one vector through X100's simplified version of TPC-H Query 1, the example from the original paper:

`SELECT returnflag, SUM((1 - discount) * extendedprice) FROM lineitem WHERE shipdate < DATE '1998-09-03' GROUP BY returnflag`

The plan is Scan, then Select, then Project, then Aggregate. Only the 4 referenced columns are scanned.

blocks.title: X100 plan for simplified Query 1 and the primitives it calls

scenes.caption: Scan produces one vector per column (shipdate, discount, extendedprice, returnflag), about 1000 values each.
Select does not copy the qualifying rows. It produces a selection vector: the positions that passed the predicate.
Project computes 1 - discount and the product only at the selected positions, writing results at the same positions. The input vectors are left untouched.
Aggregate hashes returnflag for the selected rows and adds each product to its group. After the last vector, the hash table is the answer.

blocks.title: One 8-row vector through Select, Project and Aggregate

scenes.caption: A toy vector of 8 rows (real vectors hold about 1000). Dates are month-day in 1998; the predicate is shipdate < 09-03.
select_lt_date marks rows 0, 2, 4, 5 and 7. The selection vector stores those 5 positions, sel = [0, 2, 4, 5, 7]; no data is moved.
map_sub then map_mul visit only the selected positions: (1 - 0.05) x 100 = 95, 1.00 x 50 = 50, 0.90 x 400 = 360, 0.98 x 150 = 147, 0.92 x 120 = 110.4. Unselected slots are never computed.
aggr_sum adds each product to its returnflag group: A gets 95 + 147 = 242, R gets 50, N gets 360 + 110.4 = 470.4.

blocks.md: X100's addition primitive, from the paper, shows the whole idea in a few lines. It takes the vector length, a result array, two input columns, and an optional selection vector `sel`. With `sel` it loops over the selected positions; without it, over every position. The `__restrict__` qualifiers promise the arrays do not overlap, which frees the compiler to pipeline and vectorize the loop. X100 generated hundreds of such primitives from short patterns rather than writing them by hand.

blocks.caption: The vectorized addition primitive as printed in the MonetDB/X100 paper (lightly reformatted).

blocks.title: A branch-free selection primitive building the selection vector

scenes.caption: Instead of an if, the primitive always writes i into res[k] and advances k by the comparison result (0 or 1). No branch means no misprediction when matches are random.
i = 0: 08-30 < 09-03 is true, res[0] = 0 and k becomes 1.
i = 1: 09-05 fails. res[1] = 1 is written but k stays 1, so the next write overwrites it.
i = 2 to 6: rows 2, 4 and 5 match; rows 3 and 6 do not.
i = 7: 07-31 matches. The function returns k = 5, the number of selected rows, and res holds the selection vector.

blocks.md: Primitives that each do one operation must load two inputs and store one output for one unit of work, so vectorized code tends to become load/store bound. X100 therefore also supports **compound primitives** that fuse a small expression tree (for example `(1 - discount) * price`) into one loop, passing intermediates through registers; the authors report these often ran about twice as fast as chains of single-function primitives.

A selection vector is not a filtered copy. Downstream primitives read the original vectors at the listed positions. That avoids copying, but the reads are now indirect and sparse, which matters for SIMD (next lesson).
Vectorized engines split work into type-specialized primitives over arrays, and pass filters along as lists of positions instead of moving data.

blocks.question: After Select, a vector of 1024 rows has a selection vector of length 900. The next primitive computes price x quantity. Which is the usual behavior?
options: It loops over the 900 positions in the selection vector and writes results at those same positions
It first copies the 900 rows into new contiguous vectors, then computes
It computes all 1024 rows and Select is re-applied afterwards
It switches to tuple-at-a-time for the selected rows
blocks.explain: X100 primitives accept an optional selection vector and compute only for those positions, writing at the same positions, because leaving the child's vectors intact is usually cheaper than copying the selected data.

blocks.question: Why does the branch-free select loop write res[k] = i even for rows that fail the predicate?
options: It is a bug that wastes memory
Because the selection vector must have length n
So the loop has no data-dependent branch; a failing row's write is simply overwritten by the next one
To keep the output sorted
blocks.explain: Writing unconditionally and advancing k by the 0/1 comparison result removes the branch. With unpredictable predicates this avoids branch mispredictions; the stray write is harmless since k did not advance.

lessons.title: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits

blocks.md: Primitives over flat arrays look like perfect SIMD targets. Kersten et al. tested this on an AVX-512 Skylake-X CPU, which can execute two 512-bit operations per cycle: 32 values of 32 bits per cycle, against 4 for scalar code. A selection primitive maps neatly to AVX-512: a vector compare produces a mask, and a *compress store* writes out the positions whose mask bit is set.

blocks.prompt: In a microbenchmark (8192 32-bit integers in L1 cache, dense input) the AVX-512 selection was 8.4x faster than branch-free scalar code. What speedup would you expect on the full TPC-H Query 6, where almost 90% of time is in SIMD primitives?
blocks.reveal: Only **1.4x**. From the second filter on, each selection primitive reads through a selection vector, so it must gather values from scattered positions; with 40% selectivity that limited the gain to at most 2.7x. On large data the scan is memory-bound, and below about 50% selectivity scalar and SIMD ran nearly equal. In Q6 only the first filter (selecting 43% of rows) really benefited.

blocks.title: AVX-512 selection speedup over scalar (Kersten et al., VLDB 2018)

scenes.caption: Best case: contiguous 32-bit values already in L1. Compare plus compress store gives 8.4x.
Selection vectors force sparse gathers: at 40% selectivity the gain is at most 2.7x.
In a real query, memory stalls and later sparse filters leave 1.4x end to end. SIMD helps most where data is dense and in cache.

blocks.md:
Vectorization is not the only way to kill interpretation overhead. **Data-centric code generation** (pioneered by HyPer) compiles each pipeline of the query into one tight loop that pushes a tuple through all operators while it sits in registers. Kersten et al. built both styles in one system with identical algorithms (Typer compiled, Tectorwise vectorized):

- Compiled code was 74% faster on Q1 (arithmetic-heavy, few cache misses): vectorized code executed up to 2.4x more instructions because each primitive materializes its result.
- Vectorized code was 32% faster on Q9 and 4% on Q3 (hash-join heavy): independent probes in a tight loop let the CPU overlap more cache misses.
- Overall the two were close: small gaps next to the one to two orders of magnitude the authors cite between HyPer and PostgreSQL.

blocks.title: A modern columnar scan, end to end

nodes.label:
Footer + stats
prune row groups, pages

scenes.caption: Lessons 1 and 2: read only needed columns, and use min/max stats to skip row groups and pages before any data is fetched.

Lesson 2 and 3: decode the surviving pages into flat, typed column vectors with validity bitmaps. Some engines keep dictionary or constant encodings alive in the vector (DuckDB has dictionary and constant vectors).
Lessons 4 and 5: operators pull cache-sized vectors and run primitives with selection vectors. Only the final result is assembled into rows.

blocks.md:
Where columnar engines struggle:

- **Point lookups and narrow updates.** Fetching or changing one full row touches every column; engines lean on delta stores and periodic merges.
- **Wide SELECT * results.** Tuple reconstruction at the end costs one access per column per row; late materialization helps by building rows only for survivors.
- **Small or unclustered data.** Min/max pruning needs sorted or clustered data; on random data every row group overlaps the predicate.
- **Very selective, dependent filters.** Sparse selection vectors erode SIMD gains, as the Q6 result shows.

When tuning a columnar query, check in this order: are only the needed columns read, are row groups and pages pruned (sort or cluster on common filter columns), is data dictionary-encoded where cardinality is low, and only then look at CPU-level effects like SIMD.
Columnar storage cuts bytes moved; vectorized execution cuts instructions per byte. SIMD multiplies the second only when data is dense and in cache.

blocks.question: A team's query is a long arithmetic expression over in-cache columns with almost no joins. Per Kersten et al., which engine style tends to win and why?
options: Vectorized, because it hides cache-miss latency better
Compiled (data-centric), because it keeps intermediates in registers and executes fewer instructions
Neither; Volcano tuple-at-a-time is best for arithmetic
Vectorized, because SIMD always gives 8x on arithmetic
blocks.explain: For computation-heavy, cache-resident queries like Q1, the compiled engine was 74% faster: vectorized primitives materialize every intermediate, costing extra loads, stores and instructions. Vectorized engines win on join-heavy, cache-miss-bound queries.

blocks.question: A table is written as Parquet with 1 GB row groups and no page index, written in random order. Queries filter on customer_id = X and read 3 of 50 columns. Which change most reduces bytes read?
options: Enable AVX-512 in the query engine
Increase the engine's vector size to 1M
Convert the files to Arrow IPC for storage
Sort or cluster by customer_id when writing (and write a page index) so min/max stats can skip most groups and pages
blocks.explain: Column projection already limits reads to 3 columns. The remaining waste is reading groups that cannot contain X; clustering makes min/max ranges narrow so pruning works. SIMD and vector size affect CPU, not bytes read.
